To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) uncertainty in model initial states gives rise to internal climate variability that masks and creates spurious un-forced trends in the carbon cycle and (2) the forced response of the carbon cycle can be distinguished from internal variability at decadal scales, but irreducible uncertainty remains in the carbon cycle at short timescales and small spatial scales.
uncertainty in the initial conditions of a global climate model leads to uncertainty in the simulated response of the terrestrial carbon cycle to anthropogenic forcing.
internal variability in the land carbon cycle is large and irreducible and that initial condition ensembles are needed to understand trends in the terrestrial biosphere.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the impact of internal climate variability on the terrestrial carbon cycle, and the implications for interpreting trends in the observational data record.
the role of internal variability in terrestrial carbon cycle simulations.
the question: “How does the uncertainty in model initialization affect the terrestrial carbon cycle response to climate change?”
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
internal variability in the climate system is an important source of uncertainty in climate projections.
initial-condition uncertainty produces uncertainty in climate projections because of unforced internal variability in the climate system.
the signature of internal variability is clearly evident in the terrestrial carbon fluxes simulated in CESM2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

internal variability of the climate system can be a significant source of uncertainty for climate change detection and attribution studies, and that initial-condition ensemble simulations are a necessary tool to separate forced climate change from the effects of unforced climate variability.
the internal variability in the carbon cycle is large enough to mask the anthropogenic signal in a single realization of the model and to create irreducible uncertainty in carbon cycle trends.
initial-condition ensembles are needed for both climate and carbon cycle simulations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the terrestrial carbon cycle is highly sensitive to internal climate variability, and this internal variability must be taken into account in the interpretation of carbon cycle observations and in the attribution of carbon cycle trends to climate change.
the terrestrial carbon cycle is a complex system, and the internal variability in the system can mask the forced response, especially at small scales and short times.
internal climate variability must be considered as part of the climate system response to anthropogenic forcing.
